content:
As CI is likely to be a bottleneck for CI soon, I've started collecting and analyzing stats on CI.

https://taucetiproject.github.io/TauCeti/ci/

Note also that I've adjusted CI for dynamic dispatch: we prefer using the (free) Github Runners when available, dispatching build jobs there until there are 18 concurrent runs (the maximum allowed is 20: we leave two slots unfilled so the very short running CI jobs, e.g. managing labels, interacting with zulip etc, always have headroom), and after that we overflow onto Namespace (CI machines paid for by the Lean FRO).

If anyone has a ready source of compute that we could throw into the mix for CI, please let me know. I'm working on this. But I think there is also a lot of fat we can still cut. If anyone else would like to analyze the data being collected here and help me identify CI improvements we could make, that would be great.
I'm also considering switching from the github merge queue to the bors merge queue that Mathlib uses, as I think that potentially saves a lot of builds.

An even more radical change would be to use bors-style batching even for PRs. i.e. we might do a build of PRs X and Y at the same time, and assume that if CI is good on the combination the PRs are individually fine, but then if the combined build fails we'd subdivide. This requires some careful thought about expected failure rates, in order to pick the right batch sizes.
you mean the deterministic checks on GitHub Actions being a bottleneck for CI? Saying "CI is a bottleneck for CI" makes no sense.

Coincidentally (or maybe not so coincidentally) I was looking at what time the GitHub Actions workflows is spending on, and notice some inefficiencies on the Lean untar step. That probably only cut one minute max though (5–10%?) There are probably more room for improvement.
That said, one trivial “solution” is for people to make their agent work a bit more before opening a PR? This may have an obvious downside of dividing the reviewer's attention span, and the CI would just end up getting run for less, so it's not clear whether this is a solution or merely a hack.
Another idea is to use the reviewer to also run the build (we trust reviewers anyway right?), and for merges, run on the combination only.

(I'd comment that it doesn't seem like much thought has been put into the charts. Apart from a few obvious glitch of overlapping text, it isn't at all clear why "merge queue on Namespace" (red) exist when "number of concurrent jobs" doesn't exceed the threshold)
